fields.definition: The reference signal and monitoring levels established for each input and output during soundcheck, used as the baseline settings from which the engineer mixes once the performance begins.
fields.plain_english: The volume settings the sound engineer dials in during soundcheck. They act as a starting point, so the mix is close to right the moment the show begins.
fields.purpose_function: It gives the engineer a known, repeatable starting point for gain structure and for monitor and front-of-house levels, reducing surprises and feedback risk when the show starts.
fields.practical_application: During soundcheck a technician sets input gains and fader positions per source, notes or saves them, then fine-tunes from those soundcheck levels during the actual performance.
common_mistakes: Assuming soundcheck levels will hold during the show, when a full room and energetic performers change stage volume and gain needs.
Setting levels with only one player instead of the full band, so the balance falls apart once the whole song plays.
UNSAFE: Pushing monitor or PA levels far above soundcheck settings without regard to safe hearing-exposure limits.
scenario_contexts: Setting each channel's gain and fader during a pre-show soundcheck at a club.
Recalling saved soundcheck levels on a digital console before a second night of a tour.
Adjusting up from soundcheck levels once the venue fills with an audience.

fields.definition: Sonarworks' monitor and headphone calibration software that measures the frequency response of a room and speakers, or applies a stored headphone profile, and inserts a correction filter to flatten playback toward a neutral reference response.
fields.plain_english: Software from Sonarworks that fixes the sound of your speakers or headphones. It measures how they color the sound, then evens out the tone so your mixes translate well to other systems.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to remove the tonal coloring of a room, speakers, or headphones so mixing decisions rest on a neutral reference rather than a flattering or misleading playback.
fields.practical_application: An engineer measures the room with the supplied microphone or loads a headphone model, then runs the SoundID Reference plugin on the monitor path to hear a corrected, flat response while mixing.
common_mistakes: Trusting the correction after moving the speakers or listening far off-axis, which invalidates the original measurement.
Believing correction fully fixes a bad room, when acoustic treatment is still needed for reflections and low-frequency problems.
Leaving the calibration plugin active on the output at export, so the correction is printed into the final file.
scenario_contexts: Calibrating a project-studio monitor setup before starting a mix.
Loading a headphone profile to mix while travelling.
Comparing mix translation between corrected and uncorrected monitoring.

sources: Sonarworks SoundID Reference User Manual (manufacturer technical documentation)
AES literature on loudspeaker/room equalization and monitor calibration

fields.definition: The degree to which the frequency content or tonal balance of audio stays uniform over time and between related elements, such as across sections of a song, between edited takes, or across different playback systems.
fields.plain_english: How steady the tone of a sound stays from moment to moment. If the brightness and weight do not jump around between parts, the mix has good spectral consistency.
fields.purpose_function: Keeping it steady makes a mix or edit sound cohesive and professional, so the listener is not distracted by sudden shifts in brightness, thickness, or tonal color.
fields.practical_application: A technician checks spectral consistency when comping vocal takes or matching a punch-in, using EQ or a spectrum analyzer so the joined parts share the same tonal balance.
common_mistakes: Comping takes recorded on different mics or positions without matching EQ, so the tone shifts audibly between phrases.
Judging balance only by ear on colored monitors, missing a buildup in a narrow frequency band.
Chasing a perfectly flat analyzer reading instead of a musical tonal balance.
scenario_contexts: Matching the tone of two vocal takes joined at a comp edit.
Ensuring verse and chorus guitars keep a consistent tonal balance.
Checking that a mix holds its tonal balance on phone, car, and studio speakers.

sources: AES literature on tonal balance and spectral analysis

fields.definition: In Logic Pro's Flex Time, the Speed algorithm time-stretches audio by changing playback speed like a tape machine, so the material's pitch rises or falls together with its tempo instead of being held constant.
fields.plain_english: Speed mode stretches or shrinks audio by playing it faster or slower, like speeding up a tape. When it plays faster the pitch goes up, and when it plays slower the pitch goes down.
fields.purpose_function: It provides a resampling-style, varispeed time-stretch that deliberately couples pitch to tempo, giving vintage tape character that pitch-preserving algorithms remove; it exists as a creative/FX option in the Flex Time algorithm set.
fields.practical_application: An engineer selects the Speed algorithm on a Flex-enabled region when they want tape-style pitch-and-tempo shifts on drums or effects rather than a transparent tempo change.
common_mistakes: Assuming Speed keeps the original pitch; it deliberately changes pitch with tempo, unlike the Monophonic or Polyphonic modes.
Using it on tonal, harmonic material and expecting a clean result, when it is best suited to percussive or effect sounds.
Confusing the Flex Time Speed algorithm with a global transport or project varispeed.
scenario_contexts: Speeding up a drum loop so it rises in pitch like a classic tape pull-up.
Creating a downward pitch-and-tempo drop as a transition effect.
Fitting a percussive sample to the session tempo when the retro pitch shift is wanted.

sources: Apple, Logic Pro User Guide - 'Flex Time algorithms and parameters'
David Nahmani, Apple Pro Training Series: Logic Pro (Peachpit/Apple)

fields.definition: A utility device in Reason Studios' Reason that combines several audio signals into one and splits one audio signal into several, providing a merge section (multiple inputs summed to a single output) and a splitter section (one input copied to multiple outputs).
fields.plain_english: A tool in the Reason music program that joins audio cables together or splits one into many. Think of it like a power strip for audio signals inside the software.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to work around the fixed number of jacks on Reason devices, letting you feed several sources into one input or send one output to many destinations.
fields.practical_application: On the back of the Reason rack a user patches, for example, one instrument output through the splitter to several effects, or merges several returns into a single mixer channel.
related_terms: Spider Control Voltage Merger and Splitter
common_mistakes: Confusing the merge and splitter halves and patching a source into an output jack.
Expecting the merge section to sum many hot signals cleanly without watching for clipping.
Using the audio Spider for modulation duties, which need the CV Spider instead.
scenario_contexts: Sending one synth output to three different effect chains at once.
Merging several instrument outputs into one channel for group processing.
Expanding limited device connections in a complex Reason rack.

sources: Reason Studios, Reason Operation Manual (manufacturer technical documentation)
Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers (signal distribution/splitting)

authored.term: Spider Control Voltage Merger and Splitter

fields.definition: A utility device in Reason that merges and splits control-voltage (CV) and gate signals, with a merge section that sums several CV sources into one output and a splitter section that copies one CV signal to multiple outputs, including inverted outputs for reversed modulation.
fields.plain_english: A tool in the Reason program for modulation signals, the hidden controls that move knobs by themselves. It sends one control signal to many places or combines several into one.
fields.purpose_function: It lets one modulation source, such as an LFO or envelope, drive several parameters at once, or lets several modulation sources be combined before reaching a destination.
fields.practical_application: A user patches an LFO into the CV splitter to sweep filter cutoff on several synths together, or uses an inverted output so one control opens one parameter while closing another.
common_mistakes: Patching audio through the CV Spider, which is meant for control and gate signals, not audio.
Forgetting that merged CV signals add together, producing more modulation depth than expected.
Overlooking the built-in inverted outputs and hand-patching a second reversed modulation source instead.
scenario_contexts: Driving several synth parameters from a single LFO.
Combining an envelope and an LFO into one modulation signal.
Using an inverted CV output for opposing modulation of two parameters.

sources: Reason Studios, Reason Operation Manual (manufacturer technical documentation)
Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers (control voltage/synthesis signal routing)

fields.definition: An informal term for audio that has been heavily compressed or limited so its dynamic range is greatly reduced, often to the point of audibly flattened transients and diminished punch or life.
fields.plain_english: A word for sound that has been compressed so hard it loses its punch. The loud and quiet parts get pushed to almost the same level, so it can sound flat or lifeless.
fields.purpose_function: The term flags an audible side effect of over-processing dynamics, warning that too much compression or limiting has traded transient impact and openness for loudness or consistency.
fields.practical_application: An engineer calls a drum bus or master squashed when a compressor or limiter is set too hard, then eases the ratio, threshold, or make-up gain to restore dynamics.
common_mistakes: Adding heavy master limiting for loudness and squashing the mix until it loses impact.
Confusing a squashed, over-compressed sound with a naturally dense arrangement.
Judging loudness on quiet monitors and over-compressing until the mix is squashed.
scenario_contexts: Diagnosing a lifeless master that has been limited too hard.
Describing an over-compressed drum bus during a mix review.
Comparing a dynamic mix with a squashed, loudness-maximized version.

sources: Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers (dynamic range control)
Yamaha Sound Reinforcement Handbook (compression and limiting)

fields.definition: A stage wash is a broad, even, relatively soft field of light that covers the whole stage or a large area of it, produced with wash or flood fixtures rather than tightly focused spotlights, to supply general illumination and overall colour or tone for a scene.
fields.plain_english: A stage wash is a wide, even blanket of light that covers the whole stage at once. It lights everything softly instead of pointing a tight beam at one spot.
fields.purpose_function: It provides the base layer of visibility and colour across the performance area so performers can be seen everywhere, on top of which sharper specials and spotlights are added.
fields.practical_application: A lighting technician builds a stage wash by hanging and focusing wash fixtures to blend into even coverage, often in a chosen colour, then balances specials and spots against it.
common_mistakes: Confusing a wash (broad, soft coverage) with a spot (narrow, focused beam).
Assuming 'stage wash' is an audio term; it is a stage-lighting term and appears here under a mismatched topic.
Relying on a wash alone with no specials, leaving the scene flat and without focus.
scenario_contexts: Lighting a full band evenly before adding solo spotlights.
Setting a coloured wash to establish the mood of a theatrical scene.
Providing overall even visibility across a conference stage for camera.

sources: J. Michael Gillette, Theatrical Design and Production (McGraw-Hill)
Steven Louis Shelley, A Practical Guide to Stage Lighting (Focal Press)

fields.definition: Stealth music is a low-intensity, tense music state used in games and stealth-themed media that plays while the player is sneaking or avoiding detection; it is typically quiet and sparse to convey caution, and is designed to transition into combat or alert music if the player is discovered.
fields.plain_english: Stealth music is the quiet, tense music that plays in a game while you sneak around trying not to be seen. If a guard spots you, it usually switches to louder action music.
fields.purpose_function: It reinforces the sneaking gameplay state and player caution, and serves as one node in an adaptive music system that changes with the player's situation.
fields.practical_application: A game-audio implementer sets up a stealth cue as a music state in middleware such as Wwise or FMOD, then defines transitions to combat or exploration music based on game parameters.
common_mistakes: Making stealth music too busy or loud, which undercuts the tense, quiet feel.
Failing to author smooth transitions to combat music, causing an abrupt jump when the player is detected.
Treating it as a fixed track rather than an adaptive state that responds to gameplay.
scenario_contexts: Sneaking past guards in a stealth action game.
Infiltrating a base while avoiding detection.
Switching from stealth to combat music the moment an alarm triggers.

sources: Richard Stevens & Dave Raybould, Game Audio Implementation (Focal Press)
